## Part B — mechanism cards (continued)

### B3. rkyv — generated sister types, self-relative pointers, validate-then-cast

Sources (ran): book <https://rkyv.org/format.html>, <https://rkyv.org/validation.html>, <https://rkyv.org/architecture/relative-pointers.html> (`book_src/*.md`) ·
`rkyv/src/{vec.rs,rel_ptr.rs,seal.rs,lib.rs,api/mod.rs}`, `rkyv/src/collections/swiss_table/table.rs`, `rkyv/src/collections/btree/map/mod.rs` at <https://github.com/rkyv/rkyv/tree/main/rkyv/src>.

- **What**: "total zero-copy deserialization … structuring its encoded representation so that it is the same as the in-memory representation of the source type"; access is "always just a pointer offset and a cast".
- **Sister type**: `derive(Archive)` emits `ArchivedT` where "Member types are replaced with their archived counterparts · Structs are `#[repr(C)]` · Enums have `#[repr(N)]` … choosing the smallest possible type · All primitives are replaced with versions which have stable, well-defined layouts and byte orders" (`a: u32_le, b: ArchivedString`). Build is two-step: serialize dependencies, keep a `Resolver` (their positions), then *resolve* the parent in place.
- **Format knobs are compile-time features, not bytes**: endianness, `aligned`/`unaligned`, `pointer_width_16/32/64`; defaults "Little-endian · Aligned · 32-bit relative pointers". Nothing in the buffer says which were used (no header found in the pages read).
- **Relative pointer**: "An untyped pointer which resolves relative to its position in memory" (offset from the pointer's own address); "Relative pointers don't require write access to memory either, so we can memory map entire files".
- **Root at the end**: "rkyv lays out subobjects in depth-first order from the leaves to the root. This means that the root object is stored at the end of the buffer" → "you don't need to store the position of the root object"; root = buffer length − size of the root type.
- **`ArchivedVec<T>`** = `#[repr(C)] { ptr: RelPtr<T>, len: ArchivedUsize }` (8 bytes at the 32-bit defaults — inference) over a contiguous `[Archived<T>]`.
- **`ArchivedHashMap`** = SwissTable: `ArchivedHashTable<T> { ptr: RawRelPtr, len, cap }`, one control byte per bucket (`h2 = (hash >> 57) as u8`, EMPTY `0xFF`); "The number of control bytes is rounded up to a maximum group width (16) instead of the next power of two … Since this collection is immutable after writing, we'll never benefit from having more buckets than we need." Hash is "a target-independent version of FxHash to ensure that all targets compute the same hashes".
- **`ArchivedBTreeMap<K, V, const E = 5>`** = `{ root: RelPtr<Node>, len }`; `Node { kind, keys: [K; E], values: [V; E] }`, `InnerNode { node, lesser_nodes: [RelPtr; E], greater_node: RelPtr }`, `LeafNode { node, len }`; `DEFAULT_ENTRIES_PER_NODE: usize = 5` (branching 6).
- **Validation (`bytecheck`, a default feature)**: "All pointers are checked to make sure that they: Point inside the archive · Are properly aligned · And have enough space afterward to hold the desired object", plus *subtree ranges* so "the archive follows its strict ownership model" (against "recursion attacks and memory sharing violations"); shared pointers "will fail to validate if they are different types". Cost model: one whole-archive pass before the first access (`access::<ArchivedExample, Failure>(buffer)`), "can generally be done without allocations"; the alternative is `unsafe access_unchecked` plus "checksums and cryptographic signatures".
- **Access vs deserialize**: `access` → `&ArchivedT` inside the buffer; `deserialize` / `from_bytes` → builds the native `T` (allocates, copies).
- **In-place mutation**: `access_mut` returns `Seal<'_, ArchivedT>` — "A mutable reference which may not be moved or assigned … unless it is `Unpin` and `NoUndef`", destructured with `munge` (`*value = 12345.into();`). Fixed-size fields can be overwritten; nothing can grow or be re-pointed ("rkyv supports limited in-place data mutation").
- **For static Eve**: the working proof of "derived sister type + self-relative offsets = O(1) open over mmap"; copy the resolver two-step and root-at-end. Do not copy: layout defined by the host language's type + build flags (no self-description, no evolution), and collections that are frozen at write.

### B4. FlexBuffers (schema-less FlatBuffers) and the FlatBuffers Verifier

Sources (ran): <https://flatbuffers.dev/internals/> (`docs/source/internals.md`, section "FlexBuffers"), <https://flatbuffers.dev/flexbuffers/> (`docs/source/flexbuffers.md`) ·
`include/flatbuffers/{flexbuffers.h,verifier.h,base.h}`, `rust/flexbuffers/src/builder/mod.rs`, `java/…/FlexBuffersBuilder.java` at <https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master>.

- **What**: "can also be accessed without parsing / copying / object allocation … allows unique use cases such as mmap-ing large amounts of free-form data"; "any value can be the root, including a lonely int value".
- **One offset kind**: "an unsigned integer indicating the number of bytes in a negative direction from the address of itself". Built front to back: "children are stored before parents, and the root of the data starts at the last byte" — last byte = root byte width, the byte before = root type, before that the root value (`uint8_t 13, 4, 1`). A writer can therefore stream children out and never patch.
- **Per-vector width**: "scalar data is stored with a variable number of bits (8/16/32/64). The current width is always determined by the *parent*" — one width for all elements *and* the size field (which sits "effectively at index -1"). One double widens the whole vector, hence `IndirectDouble`.
- **Type bytes**: an untyped vector is size · elements · one `uint8_t` type per element; "2 lower bits representing the bit-width of the child … 6 bits representing the actual type". Typed vectors "omit the type bytes" — only for int / uint / float / key; fixed-length 2/3/4 variants store no size.
- **Map** = values vector with three prefixes: index −3 "An offset to the keys vector (may be shared between tables)", −2 "Byte width of the keys vector", −1 size. "Both the keys and corresponding values *have* to be stored in sorted order (as determined by `strcmp`), such that lookups can be made using binary search" (`std::bsearch` in `flexbuffers.h:997`) → O(log n) get, no decode. A key is a NUL-terminated string with no size field: **string keys only**, no byte 0.
- **Sharing flags** (`flexbuffers.h:1031`): `BUILDER_FLAG_NONE = 0, BUILDER_FLAG_SHARE_KEYS = 1, BUILDER_FLAG_SHARE_STRINGS = 2, BUILDER_FLAG_SHARE_KEYS_AND_STRINGS = 3, BUILDER_FLAG_SHARE_KEY_VECTORS = 4, BUILDER_FLAG_SHARE_ALL = 7`; default `BUILDER_FLAG_SHARE_KEYS` ("By default this is on for keys, but off for strings."). Any value can be shared by hand: `builder.ReuseValue(id); // Refers to same double by offset.`
- **Doc vs code — key-vector sharing is not implemented.** C++ `EndMap` (`flexbuffers.h:1301`): "TODO(wvo): if kBuilderFlagShareKeyVectors is true, see if we can share the first vector." Rust builder: "## Not Yet Implemented - `SHARE_STRINGS` - `SHARE_KEY_VECTORS`". Java defines `BUILDER_FLAG_SHARE_KEY_VECTORS = 4` and never reads it (1 grep hit). The format permits a shared keys vector; no shipped builder emits one.
- **Limits**: widths 8/16/32/64 only; closed 6-bit type enum (no user tags); verifier size bound `FLATBUFFERS_MAX_BUFFER_SIZE` = max `soffset_t` (`base.h:342`).
- **FlexBuffers `Verifier`** (`flexbuffers.h:1844`): `reuse_tracker = nullptr, _check_alignment = true, size_t max_depth = 64`; `max_vectors_(buf_len)`; checks ranges, byte widths, `type < FBT_MAX_TYPE`, offsets, alignment, key terminators; the reuse tracker "comes at the cost of using additional memory the same size of the buffer being verified, so it is by default off".
- **FlatBuffers `Verifier::Options`** (`verifier.h:29`): `max_depth = 64` ("maximum nesting of tables and vectors"), `max_tables = 1000000`, `check_alignment = true`, `check_nested_flatbuffers = true`, `max_size = FLATBUFFERS_MAX_BUFFER_SIZE`. One full pass (vtable/field bounds, vectors, strings) before trusting accessors.
- **For static Eve**: the nearest shipped "EDN-ish tree, operable in place, minimal width per container, pooled keys". Take: root-at-end, the keys-vector / values-vector split, per-container width. Fix: string-only `strcmp` keys, no tags, key-vector sharing left as a TODO, typed vectors for four scalar kinds only.

### B5. Amazon Ion binary — in-band symbol tables, length-prefixed containers, Ion 1.1

Sources (doc read, pages downloaded): <https://amazon-ion.github.io/ion-docs/docs/binary.html> · <https://amazon-ion.github.io/ion-docs/docs/symbols.html> · Ion 1.1: <https://amazon-ion.github.io/ion-docs/books/ion-1-1/> and `…/ion-1-1/whats_new.html`.

- **What**: self-describing typed values; binary 1.0 is type-length-value — "The type descriptor octet has two subfields: a four-bit type code T, and a four-bit length L"; "If the representation is less than 14 bytes long, then L is set to the length, and the length field is omitted", else L = 14 + a VarUInt length.
- **Skip-scan, not random access**: "In Ion 1.0, all data is length prefixed. While this is good for optimizing the reading of data, it requires an Ion encoder to buffer any data in memory to calculate the data's length." A struct is "sequences of symbol/value pairs" (`field name [VarUInt] : value`). There is no offset table, so field *k* / element *i* is a linear walk that skips siblings by length (inference from the layout; the spec offers only a sorted flag: "When L is 1 … the field name integers are sorted in increasing order").
- **Symbols**: "In Ion binary, all symbols are represented as integers. These integers are symbol IDs whose corresponding text forms are defined by a symbol table."
- **Local symbol table = an in-band value**: a top-level struct annotated `$ion_symbol_table` with `imports` and `symbols:[ "rock", "paper", "scissors" ]`. **Append form**: `imports:$ion_symbol_table` — "all of the symbol ID assignments in the current symbol table are imported into the new local table" ("a local symbol table that adds two local symbols to the context"). Without it the table "resets the context".
- **Shared symbol tables**: named, versioned, fetched from a catalog. "Each import … allocates a contiguous, non-overlapping sequence of symbol IDs … The size of each import's subsequence is defined by the max_id on the import statement, regardless of the actual size of the referenced table." → local IDs stay valid when the shared table is missing or newer.
- **Segment reset**: "A value stream can contain other, perhaps different, BVMs interspersed with the top-level values. Each BVM resets the decoder to the appropriate initial state … This allows the stream to be constructed by concatenating data from different sources" (BVM = `0xE0 major minor 0xEA`).
- **Tags**: "user-defined type annotations" on any value, themselves symbols — "application-defined. Ion does not interpret".
- **Ion 1.1 status**: "This document is a working draft and is subject to change." It adds macros ("macros now enable applications to have very flexible interning of their data's structure"; "In Ion binary, macros are always addressed in E-expressions by integer macro address"), modules (symbol table + macro table), directives `set_symbols add_symbols set_macros add_macros use module import encoding`, inline symbols (`FlexSym` "makes it possible for a writer to emit any Ion value as binary without requiring a symbol table"), delimited containers ("an end marker instead of a length prefix"), and tagless-element sequences for homogeneous data.
- **For static Eve**: the best precedent for the *cache* — in-band, appendable, resettable, with importable shared tables that reserve id ranges — and for tags as interned symbols. The worst precedent for in-place work: no offsets, and 1.1's delimited containers give up even the skip.

### B6. Append-only persistent trees in a byte log — CouchDB, LMDB (the rebuttal), Bw-tree

Sources: CouchDB `main` (ran): `src/couch/src/couch_file.erl`, `src/couch/src/couch_btree.erl`, `src/docs/src/intro/overview.rst`, `src/docs/src/maintenance/compaction.rst` at <https://github.com/apache/couchdb> ·
LMDB: Chu, "MDB: A Memory-Mapped Database and Backend for OpenLDAP" <https://www.openldap.org/pub/hyc/mdb-paper.pdf> (ran `pdftotext`) · Bw-tree: Levandoski, Lomet, Sengupta, ICDE 2013 <https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/bw-tree-icde2013-final.pdf> (ran).

- **CouchDB — what an update appends**: "On-disk, CouchDB never overwrites committed data or associated structures"; "The index updates always occur at the end of the file (append-only updates)". `couch_btree:write_node` → `couch_file:append_terms`: every changed node on the path, up to a new root, is appended (node chunk threshold `DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE, 4096`).
- **CouchDB — where the root lives (code)**: the header is appended at the next 4 KiB boundary — `-define(SIZE_BLOCK, 16#1000).`, padding to `Pos rem ?SIZE_BLOCK`, then `<<1, BinSize:32/integer>>` + checksummed term. Every 4,096-byte block starts with a 1-byte prefix (1 = header, 0 = data). A reader runs `find_header(Fd, Pos div ?SIZE_BLOCK)`: scan blocks **backward from EOF** (batches of `DEFAULT_READ_COUNT, 1024`), take the newest block whose prefix is 1 and whose checksum loads (xxhash128 or md5).
- **Doc vs code**: `overview.rst` still says "The updated database header is written in two consecutive, identical chunks to make up the first 4k of the file" — the code above appends headers at the tail; the doc describes an older layout.
- **CouchDB — garbage**: none reclaimed in place. "Wasted space is recovered by occasional compaction … clones all the active data to a new file and then discards the old file"; "this requires roughly twice the disk storage".
- **LMDB — the contrast, by its author**: started from an append-only B-tree ("a meta page at the end of the database file … Any application opening the database needed to search backward from the end of the file to find the most recent meta page") and abandoned it: "With a small test database and only a few hundred add/delete operations, the DB occupied 1027 pages but only 10 pages actually contained current data; over 99% of the space was wasted."
- **LMDB — mechanism**: copy-on-write pages ("never overwrite existing data; instead the updates write to new pages"), "two meta pages occupying page 0 and page 1 of the file. They are used alternately by transactions. Each meta page points to the root node of two Btrees - one for the free list and one for the application data." Garbage: "pages that are no longer in use by any active snapshot of the database are re-used by updaters, so the database size remains relatively static"; a long reader only means "page reclaiming cannot be done".
- **Bw-tree — append as delta, not as path copy**: "Page state changes are done by creating a delta record (describing the change) and prepending it to an existing page state", installed by CAS in a mapping table that "severs the connection between physical location and inter-node links" (so a change does not propagate to the root). "Occasionally, we consolidate pages (create a new page that applies all delta changes)"; "We use a form of epoch to accomplish safe garbage collection". On flash, a log-structured store flushes only "deltas that represent the changes made to the page since its previous flush" and a cleaner reclaims old log.
- **For static Eve**: "append-only" has exactly three known garbage answers — rewrite-compact (CouchDB), a free list + reader-epoch reuse (LMDB), delta + consolidate + epoch (Bw-tree). A path-copying packed tree wastes a root-to-leaf path per write; LMDB's 1027:10 figure is the number to beat. The tail-root + backward scan is the precedent for "newest valid root in an appended byte log".

### B7. Cap'n Proto — segments, relative and far pointers, lazy validation with limits

Sources (ran, branch `v2`): `doc/encoding.md` = <https://capnproto.org/encoding.html> · `doc/cxx.md` = <https://capnproto.org/cxx.html> · `c++/src/capnp/message.h` at <https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto/tree/v2>.

- **What**: a message is "a tree of objects, with the root always being a struct"; "a "word" is defined as 8 bytes … all objects (structs, lists, and blobs) are aligned to word boundaries". "The first word of the first segment of the message is always a pointer pointing to the message's root struct" (root at the **front**).
- **Segments = arena chunks**: "If it turns out the segment you allocated isn't big enough, you can allocate additional segments without the need to relocate the data you've already written." Built "in "arena" or "region" style: each object is allocated sequentially in memory".
- **Relative pointer**: struct/list pointer offset is "in words, from the end of the pointer to the start of the struct's data section. Signed." (30 bits). **Far pointer** (cross-segment): 29-bit "Offset, in words, from the start of the target segment to the location of the far-pointer landing-pad" + 32-bit "ID of the target segment".
- **Tree, not graph**: "no more than one pointer can point at each object". No sharing inside a message.
- **Untrusted input — lazy, not up-front**: "To avoid an upfront scan of the message (which would defeat Cap'n Proto's O(1) parsing performance), validation should occur lazily when the getter method for a pointer is called".
- **Traversal limit**: `uint64_t traversalLimitInWords = 8 * 1024 * 1024;` — "The default limit is 64 MiB"; defends against "multiple pointers point at the same location … a message which is small on the wire to appear much larger when actually traversed". Stateless, so "calling the getter for the same sub-struct multiple times will cause it to be double-counted" ("it is impossible to remember whether you've seen a particular object already").
- **Nesting limit**: `int nestingLimit = 64;` (stack-overflow defense). Zero-size list elements count one word each (list amplification).
- **Canonical form**: preorder, single segment, trailing zero words truncated, not packed; "it is possible to write code which canonicalizes a Cap'n Proto message without knowing its schema". Encoders "will almost never" emit it by default.
- **Why a list cannot grow in place**: "lists of structs are represented as a flat array, not as an array of pointers. Therefore, all memory for all structs in the list must be allocated upfront." Objects are packed sequentially after it, so growth means allocate anew and abandon the old one.
- **Orphans / holes**: "An "orphan" is a Cap'n Proto object that is disconnected from the message structure"; `disownFoo()` / `adoptFoo()` relink without copying, same message only. Abandoned space stays: "if you allocate an object and then discard it, that memory is lost … The implementation will try to zero it out"; the fix is "copy the whole message tree into a fresh `MessageBuilder`".
- **For static Eve**: the precedent for multi-segment packed values with far pointers and for *lazy* bounds checks plus a work budget (the opposite of rkyv/FlatBuffers' full pre-pass). Its dead-space rule (zero, then compact by copy) is what an append-only packed form must plan for; note it zeroes, which Eve's memory model forbids.

### B8. PAX minipages and HyPer Data Blocks — columns inside one page, point access on compressed bytes

Sources (ran `pdftotext`): Ailamaki, DeWitt, Hill, Skounakis, "Weaving Relations for Cache Performance", VLDB 2001 — copy read: <https://research.cs.wisc.edu/multifacet/papers/vldb01_pax.pdf> (the canonical <https://www.vldb.org/conf/2001/P169.pdf> returned HTTP 403 here) ·
Lang et al., "Data Blocks", SIGMOD 2016 <https://db.in.tum.de/downloads/publications/datablocks.pdf>.

- **PAX — what**: "PAX groups all the values of a particular attribute together on a minipage." "Because PAX only affects layout inside the pages, it incurs no storage penalty and does not affect I/O behavior." — same page, same records as a row store, columnar *within* the page.
- **PAX page**: "Each newly allocated page contains a page header and as many minipages as the degree of the relation. The page header contains the number of attributes, the attribute sizes (for fixed length attributes), offsets to the beginning of the minipages, the current number of records on the page and the total space available on the page."
- **Two minipage kinds**: "Fixed-length attribute values are stored in F-minipages. At the end of each F-minipage there is a presence bit vector with one entry per record that denotes null values for nullable attributes." "V-minipages are slotted, with pointers to the end of each value."
- **Row view = mini-join**: "To reconstruct a record one needs to perform a mini-join among minipages, which incurs minimal cost because it does not have to look beyond the page." Record *i* = position *i* in every minipage; the header's offsets are the whole plan.
- **Data Blocks — what**: "Data Blocks are self-contained containers that store one or more attribute chunks in a byte-addressable compressed format." "Typically, we store up to 2^16 records in a Data Block" (C1).
- **Byte-addressable, on purpose**: "While many OLAP systems employ bit-packing techniques to achieve higher compression ratios, we refrain from doing so." Reason: "In case early filtering produces a sparse set of qualifying tuple positions, the cost of bit-unpacking the scan columns dwarfs …". Schemes kept: "(i) single value compression, (ii) ordered dictionary compression, and (iii) truncation", chosen "for each column in each block".
- **Point access without decompressing the block**: "Our choice for byte-aligned storage mostly avoids this penalty"; a code sits at a computable byte position, so tuple *i* of attribute *a* is one indexed load (plus a dictionary lookup) — "OLTP transactions can still quickly access individual tuples". Price, per the paper: "byte-aligned compression on average increases space consumption" versus bit-packing (factor not legible in the extracted text).
- **PSMA**: beyond min/max, "lightweight indexes called Positional SMAs (PSMAs) that narrow the scan ranges on a per-attribute basis"; "a concise lookup table that is computed when a cold chunk is "frozen" into a Data Block. Each table entry contains a scan range [b, e)", "represented as two unsigned 4-byte integers", indexed by the leading non-zero byte of (value − min).
- **For static Eve**: the two papers that already define "columnar chunk with a cheap row view". PAX: per-chunk header of column offsets + presence bits → row = same index in each column. Data Blocks: stay byte-aligned (no bit-packing) so a row view is O(1) loads; freeze-time per-column encoding choice; a positional index per column. Both assume a fixed schema per page — the heterogeneous EDN part needs B2/B4 beside them.

### B9. Row formats over bytes — Spark UnsafeRow, Fory row format + meta sharing, arrow-row

Sources (ran): `sql/catalyst/src/main/java/org/apache/spark/sql/catalyst/expressions/UnsafeRow.java` (`apache/spark` `master`) · `docs/specification/row_format_spec.md`, `xlang_serialization_spec.md` (`apache/fory` `main`) = <https://fory.apache.org/docs/specification/row_format_spec> · `arrow-row/src/lib.rs` (`apache/arrow-rs` `main`) = <https://docs.rs/arrow-row>.

- **UnsafeRow**: "An Unsafe implementation of Row which is backed by raw memory instead of Java objects. Each tuple has three parts: [null-tracking bit set] [values] [variable length portion]". "The null-tracking bit set is aligned to 8-byte word boundaries. It stores one bit per field." "In the `values` region, we store one 8-byte word per field. For fields that hold fixed-length primitive types … we store the value directly in the word. For fields with non-primitive or variable-length values, we store a relative offset (w.r.t. the base address of the row) that points to the beginning of the variable-length field, and length (they are combined into a long)." "Instances of `UnsafeRow` act as pointers to row data stored in this format." Bitset width `((numFields + 63)/ 64) * 8`.
- **Fory (ex-Fury) standard row format** — the same shape, specified: "8-Byte Alignment · Fixed-Width Field Slots: Every field uses an 8-byte slot for uniform offset calculation · Null Bitmap · Relative Offsets"; slot offset = `bitmap_size + field_index * 8`; goals "Random Field Access: Read individual fields without deserializing the entire row", "Zero-Copy Operations". A Java-only compact variant sorts fields and inlines fixed-size structs.
- **Fory meta sharing** (object-graph format, not the row format): "When meta share is enabled, TypeDef metadata is written inline the first time a type is encountered, and subsequent occurrences only reference it." `marker = (index << 1) | flag`; "`flag = 0`: new type definition follows · `flag = 1`: reference to a previously written type definition"; index is sequential in a "per-stream meta context map". A Fressian-style struct cache with an explicit define/ref bit.
- **arrow-row is not a view**: "A comparable row-oriented representation of a collection of [`Array`]. [`Row`]s are normalized for sorting, and can therefore be very efficiently compared, using `memcmp`"; "a variable length byte sequence created by concatenating the encoded form of each column". It is a *copy* into order-preserving bytes for sort/group keys; fields are not addressable by index, and "`Rows` must be generated by the same `RowConverter` for the comparison to be meaningful".
- **What makes a row view cheap** (from the three): (1) field position computable from the field index alone — fixed-width slot per field; (2) nulls in a bitmap in front, no sentinel scan; (3) variable data behind a (offset, length) pair relative to the row base, so the row relocates as bytes; (4) the "row object" is just (base, offset, size) — no per-field allocation; (5) the schema lives outside the row.
- **None of the three is a view over columnar data**: each is a materialized row buffer (Spark and Fory convert to/from columns; arrow-row converts from arrays). The in-page precedent for a view over columns is PAX's mini-join (B8) or an Arrow struct array indexed by row.
- **For static Eve**: use the UnsafeRow slot rule for homogeneous map rows *only if* rows are materialized; otherwise the row view over a column chunk is (chunk, row index) and costs nothing to make. The 8-byte-per-field slot is the price of O(1) field access without a schema-specific layout.

### B10. CBOR — tags, Packed CBOR (shared-item table), deterministic encoding; Smile back-references

Sources (ran): RFC 8949 <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8949.txt> · <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-cbor-packed/> and <https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-cbor-packed-19.txt> · <https://github.com/FasterXML/smile-format-specification/blob/master/smile-specification.md>.

- **Tags** (major type 6): "A tagged data item ("tag") whose tag number, an integer in the range 0..2^(64)-1 inclusive, is the argument and whose enclosed data item (_tag content_) is the single encoded data item that follows the head." "IANA maintains a registry of tag numbers". A decoder that does not know a tag can still hand back (number, content) (inference from the head + single-content shape) — Transit's `TaggedValue`, with integers for names.
- **Deterministic encoding, RFC 8949 §4.2.1** ("core deterministic encoding requirements"): "Preferred serialization MUST be used … arguments … MUST be as short as possible"; "Floating-point values also MUST use the shortest form that preserves the value"; "Indefinite-length items MUST NOT appear."; "The keys in every map MUST be sorted in the bytewise lexicographic order of their deterministic encodings." → one byte string per value, the precedent for canonical bytes (hash / compare without decoding).
- **Packed CBOR status**: datatracker (read 2026-11-12) shows `draft-ietf-cbor-packed-19`, "Latest revision 2026-02-02", **"Expired Internet-Draft (cbor WG) · Expired & archived"**, intended status "Proposed Standard"; the draft's footer reads "Expires 6 August 2026". -19 calls itself "a work-in-progress release". Not an RFC.
- **Packed CBOR mechanism**: two tables per active set — a shared item table and an argument table. *Item sharing*: "substructures (data items) that occur repeatedly … can be collapsed to a simple reference … The processing required during consumption is limited to following that reference". *Argument sharing*: "Data items (strings, containers) that share a prefix or suffix … can be replaced by a reference to the shared argument plus a rump data item."
- **Reference encoding**: "Simple value 0..15 → 0..15 · Tag 6(N) (unsigned integer N ≥ 0) → 16 + 2×N · Tag 6(N) (negative integer N < 0) → 16 − 2×N − 1" (zigzag, shortest first). Table setup: `Basic-Packed-CBOR = #6.113([[*shared-and-argument-item], rump])` (or `#6.1113([[*shared-item], [*argument-item], rump])`); table-building tags nest by "prepending" to the enclosing tables. Tables may also be supplied out of band.
- **Why it matters**: the stated aim is "a Packed CBOR data item that is almost as easy to consume as the original … A separate decompression step is therefore often not required" — an explicit, *transmitted* table (unlike Transit's implicit order-of-traversal cache), so references resolve without replaying the stream.
- **Smile back-references**: shared key names and (optionally) shared string values, each a "tumbling-window" buffer of 1,024 entries addressed by a 10-bit reference; only strings of "64 bytes or less" are shareable; "If it already has 1024 values, it MUST clear out buffer and start from first entry." Implicit, order-dependent (like Transit's 1,936-entry cache, A9).
- **For static Eve**: tags = integer tag ids resolved through the chunk's table; §4.2.1 = the rulebook for a canonical packed form; Packed CBOR's table-in-front + small-integer reference is the closest wire design to "chunk + its cache" for EDN-shaped data — but it is an expired draft, and CBOR itself has no offsets (sequential decode only).

### B11. Clojure incumbents — nippy, tech.ml.dataset / dtype-next, DataScript + persistent-sorted-set

Sources (ran): `taoensso/nippy` `master` (README: "Latest release: v3.9.0 (2026-09-06)"): `README.md`, `src/taoensso/nippy.clj`, `src/taoensso/nippy/impl.clj` · `techascent/tech.ml.dataset` `master`: `src/tech/v3/dataset/io/nippy.clj`, `src/tech/v3/libs/arrow.clj` · `cnuernber/dtype-next` `master`: `README.md`, `src/tech/v3/datatype/native_buffer.clj` · `tonsky/datascript` `master` `docs/storage.md` · `tonsky/persistent-sorted-set` `master`: `src-java/me/tonsky/persistent_sorted_set/{IStorage,Settings}.java`.

- **nippy custom types** (`extend-freeze` docstring): id is "ℕ∈[1, 128] - 0 byte overhead. You are responsible for managing ids." or "(Namespaced) keyword - 2 byte overhead. Keyword will be hashed to 16 bit int, collisions will throw at compile-time." Wire: `[const byte id][cust hash id][payload]` or `[cust byte id][payload]`. Readers live in a process-global `*custom-readers*` map; the payload has no length prefix in this layout, so an unknown custom type cannot be skipped (inference from the write form).
- **nippy cache**: `(cache x)` — "Wraps value so that future writes of the same wrapped value with same metadata will be efficiently encoded as references to this one … a single "foo", plus 2x single-byte references"; "Repeated keywords are cached automatically". Scope is a `with-cache` session: "ALL values frozen within a single `with-cache` body MUST be thawed together within a single corresponding `with-cache` body." Index space capped at `max-dict-count 32767`. New: `*shared-dict*` — "Experimental, subject to change … Optional shared dictionary to use when freezing/thawing", fingerprinted with FNV-1a because "these hashes go to the wire and so must be stable across JVM/Clojure/Nippy versions".
- **nippy stability promise**: "data serialized today should be readable by all future versions of Nippy" (backward only: "`vX` **may/not** be able to read all data from Nippy `vY>X`"); new types ship over "two version releases" (read, then write). But: "It has **never been an objective** of Nippy to offer **predictable byte output**" — no canonical bytes.
- **tech.ml.dataset**: nippy path = `(nippy/extend-freeze Dataset :tech.ml/dataset …)` over `dataset->data` (a decode-everything path). Arrow path: `:open-type` "Either `:mmap` or `:input-stream` defaulting to the slower but more robust `:input-stream` pathway"; "uncompressed mmap pathways typically have the highest performance - roughly 100x any other method" (the project's own figure); "Using compression makes loading via mmap non-lazy"; string dictionaries "have to be done greedily".
- **dtype-next**: "native buffers: "off-heap" container storage"; "a language independent ABI which allows zerocopy to C-based systems". A native buffer is a `long` address + datatype + length; element *i* is `address + i * width` (`adj-address`).
- **DataScript storage**: "DataScript consists of three B-trees … We store them per-node"; "`d/restore` does exactly zero reads! … restoring a database is lazy"; "one storage can only hold one database. This is because it uses constant addr to write its root." Garbage: old nodes "are still in storage" until the user runs the collector, which needs `-list-addresses` and a delete.
- **persistent-sorted-set `IStorage<Key, Address>`**: `restore(Address)` and `store(ANode)` — "For node instanceof Leaf, store node.keys() · For node instanceof Branch, store node.level(), node.keys() and node.addresses() · Generate and return new address for node". Branching factor default 512 (`branchingFactor = 512`; docs: "each node will contain 256...512 keys"); node refs default `RefType.SOFT`.
- **For static Eve**: the incumbents split the job in two — nippy = opaque sequential blob with a session cache (no in-place access, no canonical bytes); Arrow-mmap / native buffers = in-place but columnar-typed only. DataScript shows the Clojure-native shape of "persistent tree whose nodes are addressed blobs, loaded lazily" — and that its garbage is the user's problem.

### B12. Two-level containers — Zarr v3 sharding codec, HDF5 chunk cache

Sources (ran): `zarr-developers/zarr-specs` `main` `docs/v3/codecs/sharding-indexed/index.rst` = <https://zarr-specs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/v3/codecs/sharding-indexed/index.html> · `HDFGroup/hdf5` `develop` `src/H5Ppublic.h` (doc comments of `H5Pset_cache`, `H5Pset_chunk_cache`).

- **Zarr shard** = one stored object holding many inner chunks + an index. "The index contains the `offset` and `nbytes` values for each inner chunk"; index shape = chunks-per-shard + a trailing dimension of 2; "Empty inner chunks are denoted by setting both offset and nbytes to `2^64 - 1`"; "The index always has the full shape of all possible inner chunks per shard".
- **Index size is computable before reading it**: "`16 (2x uint64) * 4 (chunks per shard) + 4 (crc32c checksum) = 68 bytes`" → a reader asks the store for "the `n` first or last bytes" and then range-reads single chunks. `index_location` "must be either the string `start` or `end`. If the parameter is not present, the value defaults to `end`."
- **Write strategies named by the spec**: fixed order (replace in place, "leaving unused space"), and "**Append-only**: Any chunk to write is appended to the existing shard, followed by an updated index. If previous inner chunks are updated, their storage space becomes unused, as well as the previous index."
- **HDF5 chunk cache default — current tree**: `rdcc_nbytes` "The default size is 8 MiB per dataset."; `rdcc_nslots` "The default value is 8191." (hash slots, "should ideally be a prime number … at least 10 times the number of chunks that can fit in `rdcc_nbytes`"). The widely repeated 1 MiB / 521 slots was not found in `develop` (looked in `H5Ppublic.h`; the constants `H5D_CHUNK_CACHE_NSLOTS_DEFAULT` / `NBYTES_DEFAULT` are `SIZE_MAX` sentinels in `H5Dpublic.h`).
- **For static Eve**: a fixed-shape (offset, length) table at a known end of the container, with a sentinel for "absent" and a checksum, is the standard second level; "append chunk, then append a new index" is a spec-blessed write path whose garbage is the superseded chunk plus the superseded index.

**CPU caches** — to test "a 64 KiB chunk plus its dictionary fits L2, not L1d".

| Core | L1d | L2 (per core) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| AMD Zen 5 (EPYC 9005 "Turin") | "D-Cache: 48KB, 12-way" | "L2-Cache: 1MB, 16-way" | AMD, Hot Chips 2024 deck <https://www.hc2024.hotchips.org/assets/program/conference/day2/24_HC2024.AMD.Cohen.Subramony.final.pdf> (ran `pdftotext`). The amd.com product page failed here (HTTP/2 stream error; HTTP 503 via WebFetch). |
| Intel Granite Rapids P-core (Xeon 6) | **UNVERIFIED-HERE** (48 KB appears only in secondary pages returned by search) | "2MB L2 Cache"; I-cache "64KB, 16-way" | Intel, Hot Chips 2023 deck <https://hc2023.hotchips.org/assets/program/conference/day1/Platforms/HC2023.Intel.Gianos.v7.pdf> (ran) |
| Arm Neoverse V2 | **UNVERIFIED-HERE** (not on the page read) | "up to double the L2 cache size (2MB per core)" | <https://www.arm.com/products/silicon-ip-cpu/neoverse/neoverse-v2> (doc read) |
| Apple M4-family P-core | **UNVERIFIED-HERE** — Apple publishes no figure; secondary only: a user-posted `sysctl` readout `hw.perflevel0.l1dcachesize: 131072`, `hw.perflevel0.l2cachesize: 16777216`, `cpusperl2: 5` | same readout | <https://forums.macrumors.com/threads/request-for-some-system-information-about-cpu-caches.2478481/> (search result, not a primary source) |

Verdict on the claim: **holds for the chunk, fails for "plus its dictionary" unless the dictionary is capped far below 1 MiB.** A 65,536-byte chunk exceeds Zen 5's 48 KB L1d and fits a 1 MB or 2 MB L2. But a dictionary allowed to reach the Vortex / Parquet cap of 1 MiB (FORMATS.md C1) is by itself the whole Zen 5 L2. And if the Apple readout is right, a 64 KiB chunk fits *inside* a 128 KiB L1d there, so "not L1d" is not universal. The claim needs a stated dictionary budget (e.g. chunk + dictionary ≤ half of the smallest target L2) and a measurement per target.

### C2. Ranking — inspiration for a format that is at once (i) a Transit-like wire form for EDN-shaped data with tags and a per-chunk cache, (ii) operable in place, (iii) columnar with cheap row views

| # | Design | Why (one line) | What it lacks |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Parquet VARIANT + shredding** (the encoding, B2) | The only shipped design that does all three in one model: key dictionary + O(log n) field / O(1) index in place + typed columns shredded out of the same value. | String keys only; closed primitive set (no tags); dictionary scope = one value, not a chunk. |
| 2 | **Vortex** (A1) | Best container and columnar half: layouts, run dictionaries cut at 1 MiB / 65,535 entries, cascaded encodings, zone maps, extension dtypes, frozen editions, segment (offset, length, alignment) table. | Not a wire form for heterogeneous values; its own answer for them is #1 (`encodings/parquet-variant`). |
| 3 | **FlexBuffers** (B4) | Best in-place tree: root at end (append-friendly), width per container, keys-vector / values-vector split (a map's key vector is its shape — the hook for shredding), pooling. | No tags; `strcmp` string keys; key-vector sharing unimplemented; no columns. |
| 4 | **Arrow IPC** (B1) | Best wire framing for "chunk + dictionary": explicit dictionary messages, delta = append, no replacement in the seekable file; extension types degrade to storage; C Data Interface hand-off. | Strictly typed; heterogeneous = unions (5 bytes/value) or the variant extension. |
| 5 | **Ion** (B5) | Best cache semantics for the Transit role: in-band, appendable, resettable symbol tables; shared tables with reserved id ranges; annotations as tags; 1.1 macros = shredding at the encoding level. | No offsets (skip-scan only); 1.1 is a working draft. |

Also-rans worth one idea each: rkyv (sister types), Cap'n Proto (lazy checks + budgets), Packed CBOR (transmitted table, small-integer references), PAX / Data Blocks (row view, byte-aligned codes).

**Does "Vortex, and it isn't close" survive?** Only on axis (iii). Checked against each named rival:
- vs **Arrow IPC dictionaries** — survives as a *storage* layout (cascaded encodings, zone maps, 1 MiB coalescing); does not survive as a *wire* form: Arrow has the stream framing, delta dictionaries and the zero-copy C hand-off, and Vortex's canonical arrays are Arrow-shaped anyway.
- vs **Parquet VARIANT + shredding** — does not survive. Vortex has no native encoding for heterogeneous values; `develop` imports Arrow's `arrow.parquet.variant` and its shredding (B2). On axes (i)+(ii) for EDN-shaped data, VARIANT is the design and Vortex is its host.
- vs **FlexBuffers** — does not survive on (ii) for nested values: FlexBuffers reads any node with zero decode; Vortex's read unit is a whole segment ("Vortex never reads less than one segment") and encoded arrays need a kernel or canonicalization.
- vs **Ion** — does not survive on (i): Vortex has no in-band, appendable key/tag cache and no per-value user tags (extension dtypes are per column; the footer's id dictionary is per file).
So the honest verdict is a composition, and it is close: **VARIANT-style values (with FlexBuffers' root-at-end and shape vectors) inside a Vortex/PAX-style chunk, framed with an Arrow/Ion-style explicit, append-only cache.** No single format is the answer.

### C3. Mechanisms — best precedent for each

| Mechanism | Best precedent | How it works (2 lines) | URL |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per-chunk cache / dictionary | Arrow IPC `DictionaryBatch` (+ Ion local symbol table append) | The dictionary is its own message, defined before first use; `isDelta` appends to it; the seekable file forbids replacement, so ids are stable. Ion adds: in-band `imports:$ion_symbol_table` append, reset marker, shared tables with reserved id ranges. | <https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html> · <https://amazon-ion.github.io/ion-docs/docs/symbols.html> |
| Generated sister types | rkyv `derive(Archive)` | Emits `ArchivedT`: `#[repr(C)]`, fields swapped for archived counterparts, fixed-endian primitives, self-relative pointers; built by serialize-children-then-resolve, root last. | <https://rkyv.org/format.html> |
| Untrusted-bytes validation | Two schools: full pre-pass (rkyv `bytecheck`, FlatBuffers `Verifier`) vs lazy + budget (Cap'n Proto) | Pre-pass: bounds, alignment, ownership ranges, depth 64, ≤ 1,000,000 tables — cost O(buffer) before first read. Lazy: bounds-check each pointer at its getter, charge a traversal counter (64 MiB default), cap nesting at 64 — cost O(touched). | <https://rkyv.org/validation.html> · <https://capnproto.org/encoding.html#security-considerations> |
| Versioning / evolution | Vortex editions (A1g–i), with Ion's per-segment version marker | Magic and version are frozen forever; a release names an *edition* = the frozen set of wire ids a reader must know; writers pick an older edition for old readers. Ion: a 4-byte marker may recur mid-stream and resets decoder state. | <https://docs.vortex.dev/specs/file-format.html> · <https://amazon-ion.github.io/ion-docs/docs/binary.html> |
| Append-only mutation of packed data | CouchDB file (path copy + tail root) and Bw-tree (delta records) | CouchDB appends changed nodes then a header on a 4 KiB boundary; open = scan back for the newest checksummed header; garbage = copy-compact. Bw-tree prepends deltas, consolidates later, reclaims by epoch. LMDB is the measured warning (1027 pages for 10 live). | <https://github.com/apache/couchdb/blob/main/src/couch/src/couch_file.erl> · Bw-tree paper (B6) |
| Row view over a columnar chunk | PAX minipages (+ Data Blocks byte-aligned codes) | Chunk header holds each column's offset and width; presence bits per column; row *i* = element *i* of every column ("mini-join … does not have to look beyond the page"). Byte-aligned codes keep each field one load. | <https://research.cs.wisc.edu/multifacet/papers/vldb01_pax.pdf> · <https://db.in.tum.de/downloads/publications/datablocks.pdf> |
| Pre-mapped placement (consumer places without planning) | Vortex footer `SegmentSpec { offset: uint64; length: uint32; alignment_exponent: uint8 }` (A1f); Zarr shard index; safetensors header (A7) | Every unit's offset, length and required alignment are in one small table read first (Zarr: 16 bytes × chunks + 4, size known in advance), so the reader allocates and reads each unit straight to its final aligned place. (Vortex's ≥ 64 KB tail read is guaranteed to cover the postscript, which locates the footer.) | <https://github.com/vortex-data/vortex/blob/develop/vortex-file/flatbuffers/vortex-file/footer.fbs> · <https://zarr-specs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/v3/codecs/sharding-indexed/index.html> |
